tagline: Two mountain notches link trading routes, summit railways and grand hotels.
intro: The Presidential Range Tour links Pinkham and Crawford notches on a circuit from Littleton through the White Mountains. Visit NH highlights mountain views and year-round recreation along its 115-mile itinerary. At Pinkham, the road enters a valley shaped by ice; through Crawford, US 302 follows the Saco River between steep sides. Across Crawford’s high point, the drainage changes: the Saco flows south through the notch, while Crawford Brook flows northwest toward the Ammonoosuc River and the Connecticut watershed.

Crawford Notch carried commerce before the scenic tour: the Tenth New Hampshire Turnpike was extended through it to Lancaster in 1803. The turnpike and the later railroad gave settlers northwest of the mountains a route toward coastal trading ports. When the Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad opened through the notch in 1875, it brought tourists in large numbers, and resort hotels followed.

Begin in Littleton, taking NH 116 to Whitefield and US 3 to Lancaster. US 2 continues through Jefferson and Randolph, where the Presidential Range comes into view. Turn south on NH 16 through Pinkham Notch and Jackson, then west on US 302 into Bartlett. The return leads through Crawford Notch, past the Mount Washington Hotel, and through Twin Mountain and Bethlehem toward Littleton.
notice: In Pinkham Notch, Mount Washington rises more than 4,000 feet above the valley floor.

moments.title: Mount Washington Cog Railway
moments.text: On a clear day, smoke from the Cog Railway is visible from Route 2 as the train climbs Mount Washington’s western side. Sylvester Marsh developed the railway after climbing the mountain in 1852. His 1858 charter preceded construction, which the Civil War delayed until 1866. Paying passengers began riding in 1868, before the tracks reached the summit in July 1869. The world’s first mountain-climbing cog railway uses a ladder-like rack whose open rungs engage the cog wheel’s teeth. The openings let snow and debris fall through. Steam and biodiesel locomotives now share the railway’s work.

moments.title: Pinkham Notch
moments.text: Mount Washington rises more than 4,000 feet above the floor of Pinkham Notch, opposite the Wildcat Range. The Laurentide Ice Sheet changed a river’s V-shaped valley into the U-shaped passage that Route 16 now serves. Two rivers carry water away in opposite directions: the Ellis drains the south end, and the Peabody drains the north. The visitor center also has an earlier life beneath its present role: in 1921, the Appalachian Mountain Club converted a logging camp near the height of land into the Pinkham Notch Visitor Center. At the notch’s lowest elevations, sugar maple, American beech and yellow birch dominate the hardwood forest.

moments.title: Mount Washington Hotel
moments.text: Joseph Stickney’s Mount Washington Hotel opened in 1902, with granite and stucco masonry worked by Italian artisans. The Y-shaped building took shape from 1900 and opened on July 28, 1902. Its later role reached far beyond mountain vacations: the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference held here led to the establishment of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in 1945. The hotel survives among the White Mountains’ remaining grand hotels, at the northern end of Crawford Notch along US 302. It was seasonal until 1999, when replacement windows and an overhaul prepared it for its first winter season.
